nameStory: The 'greater snowdrop' gets its name from being larger and more robust than its close cousin, the common snowdrop. Both species earn the 'snowdrop' name from their pure white, teardrop-shaped flowers that dangle like drops of snow from slender stems. This particular species honors Henry John Elwes, a Victorian-era botanist and plant collector who was passionate about bulbs and helped introduce many snowdrop varieties to British gardens.
description: Greater snowdrop is a small but sturdy spring bulb that grows 8-10 inches tall from an underground bulb about the size of a large marble. It produces two blue-green, strap-like leaves and a single white flower that hangs gracefully from the tip of each stem like a tiny lantern. The flower is distinctively bell-shaped with white petals marked by green patches, creating an elegant early spring display. This European native has found a home in New England gardens and occasionally spreads beyond cultivation.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single white, bell-shaped flower hangs from each stem, about 1 inch long with distinctive green markings both at the tip and base of the inner petals - touch the papery petals and they feel delicate but waxy

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two flat, strap-shaped leaves per bulb with a distinctive blue-green color and smooth, waxy texture that feels cool and slightly thick to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Emerges from underground bulb in early spring, typically 8-10 inches tall and more robust-looking than other snowdrop species, often forming small colonies over time

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flowers nod downward on solid green stems and have no scent, but the green markings form distinctive patterns - two green patches on each of the inner three petals

habitat: In New England, greater snowdrop is primarily found in cultivated settings like old gardens, cemeteries, and around historic home sites where it has been planted and naturalized. It occasionally escapes cultivation and can be found in nearby woodlands, along stone walls, or in areas with rich, well-draining soil that stays moist in spring but dries somewhat in summer. Look for it in partially shaded areas under deciduous trees.

seasonality.spring: Flowers appear in late February through March, often pushing up through snow - the entire plant emerges and blooms within a few weeks, making it one of our earliest spring bloomers.
seasonality.summer: Leaves persist into late spring before dying back completely, leaving no trace above ground as the plant goes dormant until next year.
seasonality.fall: Completely dormant with no visible parts above ground, though the bulb is developing next year's flower underground.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground growth visible, but in mild winters or late winter warm spells, you might spot the first green shoots pushing through mulch or snow.

funFact: Snowdrop bulbs contain a compound called galantamine that's now used as a treatment for Alzheimer's disease - this humble garden flower has become an important source for modern medicine, with tons of bulbs harvested annually for pharmaceutical use.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common snowdrop, but greater snowdrop is noticeably larger and more robust overall, with broader leaves and bigger flowers. Memory trick: 'greater' means bigger in every way - taller stems, wider leaves, and more substantial flowers that seem to have more presence in the garden.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'greater snowdrop,' this species is actually less common in New England than the regular snowdrop, appearing mainly in specialty gardens or collections. Many gardeners don't realize there are different snowdrop species and may have either type growing without knowing which one they have.
compareHints: Greater snowdrop is larger and more robust than common snowdrop (Galanthus nivalis) in all aspects - taller stems, broader leaves, and bigger flowers. While common snowdrop typically grows 4-6 inches tall with narrow leaves, greater snowdrop reaches 8-10 inches with distinctly broader, more blue-green foliage. The green markings on the flowers are also more prominent and extensive in greater snowdrop.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common snowdrop is smaller and more delicate than its relatives greater snowdrop and green snowdrop, both of which are taller and less commonly encountered in New England.
Green snowdrop differs from common snowdrop by having broader, blue-green leaves and a single green mark on the inner petals rather than two.
